title: Research Bite #70: From Teacher Quality to Teaching Quality: Instructional Productivity and Teaching Practices
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #70 covers Simon Briole's 'From teacher quality to teaching quality: Instructional productivity and teaching practices,' published in Economics of Education Review (2026), building on an earlier working paper version. Using TIMSS 2011 data and a within-student, across-topic design (comparing the same student's outcomes across four different maths topics taught by the same teacher), Briole isolates instructional time from confounds like pupil ability and fixed teacher quality. The headline effect: each additional weekly hour of instruction on a topic raised that topic's test scores by about 4.3% of a standard deviation in the US sample. But the paper's more important finding is about variation in that return -- an hour taught by a teacher who emphasized active student participation and discussion was worth roughly twice as much as an hour taught through lecturing and independent seatwork. Instructional time, in other words, is not a fixed-value input; its productivity depends heavily on how the time is used.
points: The within-student, across-topic design is methodologically clever: by comparing the same student across different topics taught by the same teacher, Briole strips out both pupil-ability and teacher-quality confounds that plague simpler instructional-time studies.

The finding that active-participation teaching roughly doubles the productivity of instructional time reframes the 'more time on task' policy lever: simply adding hours is a weaker intervention than changing how those hours are taught.

A 4.3% standard-deviation gain per weekly hour gives schools a concrete, if modest, unit of value for scheduling decisions -- useful for weighing tradeoffs when adding instructional time to one subject means subtracting it from another.

Because the effect is topic-specific (comparing the same teacher across topics), the finding speaks directly to curriculum sequencing and time allocation within a single teacher's practice, not just cross-teacher comparisons.
The result adds empirical weight to active-participation pedagogy debates: this is a causal estimate of return on instructional time, not just a correlational preference survey about teaching style.
